newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Nobel laureate could have been humble vet.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Nobel laureate could have been humble vet.

text.p: Australian immunologist Peter Doherty, joint winner of the 1996 Nobel prize for medicine, very nearly became a humble country vet.
But an interest in animal pathology led him to start experiments on the immune systems of mice -- experiments which set him on a path that created medical history.

"I went to the local veterinary school, not to the medical school, and I thought for a long time that I'd be a sort of country vet," Doherty, 55, told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio after news that he would share the prize with Switzerland's Rolf Zinkernagel.
"So it's not really what I expected to do with my life, but that's just the way it turns out."

The A$1.44 million prize was awarded jointly to Doherty and Zinkernagel for a chance discovery over twenty years ago showing how the immune system in mice could recognise and kill virus-infected cells.
The findings give hope for the treatment of diseases such as cancer, diabetes and AIDS.

With a veterinary science degree and a doctorate in animal pathology under his belt, Doherty researched viral infections infections in mice with Zinkernagel at the John Curtin School of Medical Research in Canberra from 1972 to 1975.
School Director Kevin Lafferty said they were working on mice and how the immune system got rid of viruses.
"It led through to all sorts of applications in human immunology," Lafferty told Reuters.
Doherty's is not the first Nobel given for work at the Canberra institute, which is part of the Australian National University.
The school was set up in 1958 by another Nobel laureate, Howard Florey, who won the prize in 1945 for his pioneering work on penicillin. Neuroscientist Jack Eccles won it in 1963.
Doherty said that because the research was so central to the way the immune system worked they realised it was an important discovery.
Articles on their findings were published in science journal Nature in 1974 and in the The Lancet the following year.

"It really laid out what we thought the implications were and the reason we've won the Nobel Prize is what were essentially at that time a number of informed guesses which actually turned out to be correct," Doherty said.
He said they had uncovered the key to the whole transplantation system and why grafts were rejected from one person to another.
Doherty is head of immunology at St Jude's Children's Research Hospital in Tennesee and professor of pediatrics and pathology at the University of Tennesee, Memphis.
